Imagine you are analyzing a historical rocket launch and a coastal lighthouse. The audio recording mentions a specific launch site, and the image shows a distinct lighthouse. First, identify the launch site from the audio and the lighthouse from the image. Then, using this information:

1. Calculate the great-circle distance (in kilometers, rounded to the nearest whole number) between the launch site and the lighthouse.
2. Find the maximum altitude (in km) reached by the type of rocket typically launched from that site, and determine the lighthouse's focal plane height (in feet) and its nominal range (in nautical miles). Convert the lighthouse's nominal range to kilometers.
3. Assuming a spherical Earth with an average radius, determine whether an observer at the lighthouse (at its focal plane height) would have a direct line of sight to the rocket if it were at its maximum altitude directly above the launch site. Show your calculations using the horizon distance formula.
4. Explain why the lighthouse's light would not be visible from the launch site, even if the rocket might be seen from the lighthouse.
answer: 1. Great-circle distance: 713 km. 2. Rocket maximum altitude: 600 km; Lighthouse focal plane height: 88 ft (0.0268 km); Lighthouse nominal range: 13 nautical miles = 24.1 km. 3. Yes, the rocket would be visible from the lighthouse because the sum of horizon distances (2847.8 km) exceeds the great-circle distance (713 km). 4. The lighthouse's light would not be visible from the launch site because its nominal range is only 24.1 km, which is far less than the 713 km distance between the locations.

## Identification

**Launch site (audio):** The commentator says *"This is Wallops Launch Control… the Black Brant 9 suborbital sounding rocket as part of the DYNAMO‑2 mission… Dr. Rob Pfaff and his team."* → **NASA Wallops Flight Facility, Wallops Island, Virginia** (37.933° N, 75.468° W). Rocket type: **Black Brant IX** (Terrier–Orion, two‑stage).

**Lighthouse (image):** White cylindrical tower with a black lantern room on a small rocky islet, attached white keeper's dwelling with a red roof, a small white house and a little red outbuilding, gulls and granite ledges in the foreground → **Cape Neddick Light, "The Nubble," York, Maine** (43°09′54.7″ N, 70°35′27.9″ W). Wikipedia/USCG data: tower 41 ft, **focal plane 88 ft**, **nominal range 13 nmi**.

---

## 1. Great‑circle distance

Haversine with R = 6371 km: Δσ = 6.409° → **d ≈ 713 km** (443 mi). *(Using the exact pad location instead of the main base changes this by <2 km.)*

## 2. Key figures

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Black Brant IX maximum flight height | **300 km** |
| Nubble focal plane height | **88 ft** = 26.8 m = 0.0268 km |
| Nubble nominal range | **13 nmi** = 13 × 1.852 = **24.08 km** (≈24.1 km) |

## 3. Line of sight? — YES

Horizon distance formula: **d = √(2Rh)**

- From the rocket at 300 km: d₁ = √(2 × 6371 × 300) = √3,822,600 ≈ **1955 km**
- From the lamp at 0.0268 km: d₂ = √(2 × 6371 × 0.0268) = √341.9 ≈ **18.5 km**
- Maximum mutually visible ground separation: 1955 + 18.5 ≈ **1974 km**

Since **713 km ≪ 1974 km**, a direct line of sight exists — with a margin of ~1260 km. Equivalently, the rocket would need to be only **h_min = (713 − 18.5)²/(2 × 6371) ≈ 38 km** high to peek over the Nubble's horizon; at 300 km it is far above that. Exact spherical geometry puts the rocket at an **elevation of ≈19° above the horizon** as seen from the Nubble, at a slant range of ≈788 km. (This is why Wallops Black Brant plumes are routinely reported from New England — e.g., the 2009 Black Brant noctilucent cloud seen across the northeast.)

## 4. Why the lighthouse beam can't be seen from Wallops

1. **Curvature blocks it completely.** The lamp's beam travels in a straight line tangent to the spherical Earth only 18.5 km out; its horizon dip is just 0.17°. For a Wallops observer (eye ≈2 m, own horizon ≈5 km), the target height needed to be seen at 713 km is ≈**(713 − 5)²/(2 × 6371) ≈ 39 km** — the 88‑ft light would have to be ~1,450× higher. The Earth itself is in the way, whereas the rocket is *above* the atmosphere, outside the obscuring bulge.
2. **Range deficit.** Nominal range is 24.1 km vs. a 713 km separation — the light is specified to reach only ~1/30th of the distance.
3. **Inverse‑square fading.** Even ignoring curvature, flux falls as (24.08/713)² ≈ 1.1 × 10⁻³ — about **1/870** of the intensity at its rated range, on an already faint (4th‑order Fresnel, ~10,000 cd) rotating beacon.
4. **Atmospheric extinction.** Those 713 km lie entirely inside the dense lower atmosphere (haze, aerosols, Rayleigh scattering, curvature‑following fog layers), which removes orders of magnitude more light — while the rocket at 300 km sits in near‑vacuum with a sunlit, glowing exhaust plume.

**Asymmetry in one line:** the rocket is a bright object lifted *above* the Earth's shadow by 300 km; the lighthouse is a weak source confined *below* the horizon by 18.5 km of curvature and 24 km of rated range.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Family of Canadian-designed sounding rockets

[![Image 4]]

Black Brant sounding rockets

The **Black Brant** is a family of [Canadian]-designed [sounding rockets] originally built by [Bristol Aerospace], since absorbed by [Magellan Aerospace] in [Winnipeg], Manitoba. Over 800 Black Brants of various versions have been launched since they were first produced in 1961, and the type remains one of the most popular sounding rockets.[[1]]#cite_note-1) They have been repeatedly used by the [Canadian Space Agency] and [NASA].

## History

[[edit]&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Black Brant was the result of research at [Canadian Armament Research and Development Establishment] (CARDE) during the 1950s into the nature of the upper part of the [atmosphere] as part of ongoing research into [anti-ballistic missile] systems and very-long-range communication. In 1957, CARDE contracted Bristol to produce a simple [rocket][fuselage], called the **Propulsion Test Vehicle**, for studies into high-power [solid fuels]. The resulting design, by [Albert Fia], was quite heavy, as it was designed to be able to accommodate a wide variety of engine burning times, propellant loadings and launch angles in keeping with its role as a test vehicle for ABM systems development. The first test flight took place only two years later from the [Churchill Rocket Research Range] in September 1959.[[2]]#cite_note-:0-2)

CARDE's attention later turned to long-distance communications and they found the _Propulsion Test Vehicle_ system useful as a [sounding rocket]. To better suit this role, Bristol modified the design to be lighter and more tailored to the sounding rocket role. This became the Black Brant,[[2]]#cite_note-:0-2) sharing the name with the [Black Brant] "Brant (goose)") goose. CARDE launched a number of Black Brant rockets over the next few years, both the original _Black Brant I_ design which could place a 68 kg (150 lb) payload to 150 km (93 mi) altitude, as well as the larger _Black Brant II_ which first flew in October 1960, and the smaller but higher-altitude _Black Brant III_.

The rocket's design emphasized reliability over payload and range.[[3]]#cite_note-ley196406-3) In July 1963 the much larger _Black Brant V_ first flew, which was also used as a booster stage for the _Black Brant III_ to make the _Black Brant IV_. The IV first flew in 1964, but failed, as did the next test launch. Aside from these two launches, which were corrected for, the Black Brant has never had another failure, making it one of the most reliable rockets in history. Since then it has undergone continual evolution, and the current versions are the XI and XII, consisting of Black Brant V used as an upper stage, with [Talos] and [Terrier] boosters as lower stages. They have reached altitudes of more than 1,500 km (930 mi), which is above the [ionosphere] and well above the orbits of the [Space Shuttle] and the [International Space Station].

The propellant designs developed by CARDE in the Black Brant program were the highest performing solid fuels of their day. Bristol then placed this propellant in a new 70 mm (2.8 in) rocket to form the [CRV7],[[4]]#cite_note-4) the first rocket capable of penetrating standard [Warsaw Pact] aircraft hangars. The CRV7 has since gone on to become the de facto standard rocket for most Western-aligned militaries.

In 1976, Australia and Canada through the [National Research Council Canada] (NRCC) agreed[[5]]#cite_note-5) to launch a rocket from [Woomera Test Range]. The Black Brant VB rocket was launched there on 9 November for experiments in the ionosphere.[[6]]#cite_note-6) Later, NASA would launch a number of Black Brant IX.

At present, due to its 98% success rate, it remains one of the most popular sounding rockets ever built. The rockets have been used repeatedly by the [Canadian Space Agency] and NASA. There is a 1:1 scale model of the Black Brant IX rocket in front of the head office of the Canadian Space Agency in Saint-Hubert, east of [Montréal]. A full-scale Black Brant VC is on display in the Science Gallery of The [Manitoba Museum] in [Winnipeg], Manitoba, [Canada], and a Black Brant IV B replica is located at the [Royal Aviation Museum of Western Canada] also in Winnipeg.[[7]]#cite_note-7)

In 1995, a Black Brant XII four-stage sounding rocket from the [Andøya Rocket Range] off the northwestern coast of Norway caused the [Norwegian rocket incident], also known as the Black Brant scare. The trajectory resembled that of a U.S. Navy submarine-launched [Trident missile] "Trident (missile)"). Russian nuclear forces were put on high alert as a result, fearing a high-altitude nuclear attack that could blind Russian radar, and Russia's "nuclear briefcase", the [Cheget], was brought to Russian president [Boris Yeltsin],[[8]]#cite_note-8) who then had to decide whether to launch a retaliatory nuclear strike against the United States. It is the first and thus far only known incident where any nuclear-weapons state had its nuclear briefcase activated and prepared for launching an attack.

On September 19, 2009, a Black Brant XII that was launched to study clouds caused numerous calls from the northeastern U.S. reporting "strange lights in the sky". NASA reported that the light came from an artificial [noctilucent cloud] formed by the exhaust particles of the rocket's fourth stage at an altitude of about 278 km (173 mi).[[9]]#cite_note-9)

**Wallops Flight Facility** (**WFF**; [IATA]: **WAL**, [ICAO]: **KWAL**, [FAA][LID]: **WAL**) is a [rocket launch site] on [Wallops Island] on the [Eastern Shore of Virginia], [United States], just east of the [Delmarva Peninsula] and approximately 100 miles (160 km) north-northeast of [Norfolk]. Since May 2026, the facility has been operated by the [John F. Kennedy Space Center] in [Merritt Island, Florida], having previously been operated by the [Goddard Space Flight Center] in [Greenbelt, Maryland][[1]]. WFF primarily serves to support science and exploration missions for [NASA] and other [federal agencies]. WFF includes an extensively instrumented range to support launches of more than a dozen types of [sounding rockets];[[2]] small expendable suborbital and orbital rockets;[[3]][high-altitude balloon] flights carrying scientific instruments for atmospheric and astronomical research; and, using its Research Airport, [flight tests] of aeronautical research aircraft, including [unmanned aerial vehicles].

There have been over 16,000 launches from the rocket testing range at Wallops since its founding in 1945 in the quest for information on the flight characteristics of airplanes, launch vehicles, and spacecraft, and to increase the knowledge of the Earth's upper atmosphere and the environment of [outer space]. The launch vehicles vary in size and power from the small [Super Loki] meteorological rockets to orbital-class vehicles.[[4]][[5]][[6]]

The Wallops Flight Facility also supports science missions for the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration] (NOAA) and occasionally for foreign governments and commercial organizations. Wallops also supports development tests and exercises involving [United States Navy] aircraft and ship-based electronics and weapon systems in the [Virginia Capes] operating area, near the entrance to the [Chesapeake Bay]. In addition to its fixed-location instrumentation assets, the WFF range includes mobile [radar], [telemetry] receivers, and command transmitters that can be transported by [cargo planes] to locations around the world, in order to establish a temporary range where no other instrumentation exists, to ensure safety, and to collect data in order to enable and support suborbital rocket launches from remote sites.

The WFF mobile range assets have been used to support rocket launches from locations in the Arctic and Antarctic regions, [South America], Africa, Europe, [Australia], and at sea. Workers at Wallops include approximately 1,000 full-time NASA [civil service] employees and the employees of contractors, about 30 [U.S. Navy] personnel, and about 100 employees of NOAA.

## History

[[edit]]

In 1945, NASA's predecessor agency, the [National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics] (NACA), established a rocket launch site on [Wallops Island] under the direction of the [Langley Research Center]. This site was designated the **Pilotless Aircraft Research Station** and conducted high-speed aerodynamic research to supplement wind tunnel and laboratory investigations into the problems of flight. In 1958, Congress established NASA, which absorbed Langley Research Center and other NACA field centers and research facilities. At that time, the Pilotless Aircraft Research Station became a separate facility, **Wallops Station**, operating directly under NASA Headquarters in Washington, D.C.

In 1959, NASA acquired the former **Naval Air Station Chincoteague**, and engineering and administrative activities were moved to this location. In 1974, the Wallops Station was named **Wallops Flight Center**. The name was changed to **Wallops Flight Facility** in 1981, when it became part of Goddard Space Flight Center.

In the early years, research at Wallops concentrated on obtaining aerodynamic data at transonic and low supersonic speeds. Between 1959 and 1961, Project Mercury[[7]] capsules were tested at Wallops in support of NASA's crewed space flight program – the [Mercury program] – before astronauts were launched from [Cape Canaveral Air Force Station] in Florida. Some of these tests using the [Little Joe] "Little Joe (rocket)")[booster rocket] were designed to [flight-qualify] components of the spacecraft, including the escape and recovery systems and some of the life support systems. Two rhesus monkeys, [Sam], launched in 1959, and Miss Sam, 1960, were sent aloft as pioneers for astronauts; both were recovered safely.

The first payload launched into orbit from Wallops Island was [Explorer IX], atop a [Scout rocket], on February 15, 1961.[[8]]

On September 6, 2013, the Lunar Atmosphere and Dust Environment Explorer ([LADEE]) was launched from Wallops, atop a [Minotaur V] rocket. This was the first time that an American lunar mission had been launched from anywhere but [Florida].[[9]]

In May 2026, [NASA Administrator][Jared Isaacman] announced that operational control of the Wallops Flight Facility would be moved from Goddard Space Flight Center to the John F. Kennedy Space Center.[[10]]

Wallops Island is currently experiencing [beach erosion] of 10 to 22 feet (3 to 7 meters) a year, due in part to the [current sea level rise]; some access roads and parking lots have had to be rebuilt several times over the past five years. NASA has responded by continually fortifying the shoreline with sand.[[11]]

A permanent ground control station for NASA's [RQ-4 Global Hawk] drone is at Wallops Flight Facility.[[12]]

## Facilities

[[edit]]

[![Image 8]]

The WFF Main Base is located on the Eastern Shore of Virginia on the [Delmarva Peninsula] about 5 miles (8.0 km) west of [Chincoteague, Virginia]; about 90 miles (140 km) north of [Norfolk, Virginia], and 40 miles (64 km) southeast of [Salisbury, Maryland]. The WFF consists of three separate parcels of land totaling 6,200 [acres] (25 km²): the Main Base, the Mainland, and the Wallops Island Launch Site. The Mainland and the Wallops Island Launch Site are about 7 miles (11 km) southeast of the Main Base.

### Airspace

[[edit]]

Wallops operates [controlled airspace] with [Federal Aviation Administration] (FAA) qualified [air traffic controllers] including:

* The WFF Airport Control Zone to 2,500 feet (760 m) within a 5-statute-mile (8.0 km) radius of the airport
* Restricted Area R-6604 connecting WFF airspace and offshore warning areas.

### Fixed facilities

[[edit]]

Major Wallops facilities include FAA-certified [runways]; an experimental UAV runway; and crash, fire, and rescue services. WFF has facilities for the receipt, inspection, assembly, checkout and storage of [rocket motors] and other hazardous [pyrotechnic devices]. The Wallops Island Launch Site includes six [launch pads], three [blockhouses] for launch control, and assembly buildings to support the preparation and launching of suborbital and orbital launch vehicles.

{{short description|Family of Canadian-designed sounding rockets}}
[[File:Black Brant sounding rockets shapes-01.jpg|thumb|Black Brant sounding rockets]]
The '''Black Brant''' is a family of [[Canada|Canadian]]-designed [[sounding rocket]]s originally built by [[Bristol Aerospace]], since absorbed by [[Magellan Aerospace]] in [[Winnipeg]], Manitoba. Over 800 Black Brants of various versions have been launched since they were first produced in 1961, and the type remains one of the most popular sounding rockets.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://magellan.aero/product/rockets/black-brant-rockets/ |title=Black Brant Rockets |publisher=Magellan Aerospace |access-date=12 October 2020 |archive-date=13 July 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190713130901/http://magellan.aero/product/rockets/black-brant-rockets/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> They have been repeatedly used by the [[Canadian Space Agency]] and [[NASA]].

==History==
Black Brant was the result of research at [[DRDC Valcartier|Canadian Armament Research and Development Establishment]] (CARDE) during the 1950s into the nature of the upper part of the [[Earth's atmosphere|atmosphere]] as part of ongoing research into [[anti-ballistic missile]] systems and very-long-range communication. In 1957, CARDE contracted Bristol to produce a simple [[rocket]] [[fuselage]], called the '''Propulsion Test Vehicle''', for studies into high-power [[Solid-fuel rocket|solid fuel]]s. The resulting design, by [[Albert Fia]], was quite heavy, as it was designed to be able to accommodate a wide variety of engine burning times, propellant loadings and launch angles in keeping with its role as a test vehicle for ABM systems development. The first test flight took place only two years later from the [[Churchill Rocket Research Range]] in September 1959.<ref name=":0">{{cite web |url=https://www.designation-systems.net/dusrm/app4/blackbrant.html |title=Black Brant 2B |publisher=Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles |access-date=5 August 2015}}</ref>

CARDE's attention later turned to long-distance communications and they found the ''Propulsion Test Vehicle'' system useful as a [[sounding rocket]]. To better suit this role, Bristol modified the design to be lighter and more tailored to the sounding rocket role. This became the Black Brant,<ref name=":0" /> sharing the name with the [[Brant (goose)|Black Brant]] goose. CARDE launched a number of Black Brant rockets over the next few years, both the original ''Black Brant I'' design which could place a {{convert|68|kg|abbr=on}} payload to {{convert|150|km|abbr=on}} altitude, as well as the larger ''{{nowrap|Black Brant II}}'' which first flew in October 1960, and the smaller but higher-altitude ''{{nowrap|Black Brant III}}''.

The rocket's design emphasized reliability over payload and range.<ref name="ley196406">{{Cite magazine|last=Ley|first=Willy|date=June 1964|title=Anyone Else for Space?|department=For Your Information|url=https://archive.org/stream/Galaxy_v22n05_1964-06_modified#page/n69/mode/2up|magazine=Galaxy Science Fiction|pages=110–128}}</ref> In July 1963 the much larger ''{{nowrap|Black Brant V}}'' first flew, which was also used as a booster stage for the ''{{nowrap|Black Brant III}}'' to make the ''{{nowrap|Black Brant IV}}''. The IV first flew in 1964, but failed, as did the next test launch. Aside from these two launches, which were corrected for, the {{nowrap|Black Brant}} has never had another failure, making it one of the most reliable rockets in history. Since then it has undergone continual evolution, and the current versions are the XI and XII, consisting of {{nowrap|Black Brant V}} used as an upper stage, with [[RIM-8 Talos|Talos]] and [[RIM-2 Terrier|Terrier]] boosters as lower stages. They have reached altitudes of more than {{convert|1500|km|abbr=on}}, which is above the [[ionosphere]] and well above the orbits of the [[Space Shuttle]] and the [[International Space Station]].

The propellant designs developed by CARDE in the {{nowrap|Black Brant}} program were the highest performing solid fuels of their day. Bristol then placed this propellant in a new {{convert|70|mm|abbr=on}} rocket to form the [[CRV7]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=Government of Canada, Defence Research and Development Canada, Director Research and Development Communications |title=Archives |url=http://www.drdc-rddc.gc.ca/news-nouvelles/archives/spotlight-pleinfeux/0307-eng.asp |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110706181715/http://www.drdc-rddc.gc.ca/news-nouvelles/archives/spotlight-pleinfeux/0307-eng.asp |archive-date=2011-07-06 |access-date=2026-07-10 |website=www.drdc-rddc.gc.ca |language=en}}</ref> the first rocket capable of penetrating standard [[Warsaw Pact]] aircraft hangars. The CRV7 has since gone on to become the de facto standard rocket for most Western-aligned militaries.

In 1976, Australia and Canada through the [[National Research Council Canada]] (NRCC) agreed<ref> {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170415112955/http://www3.austlii.edu.au/au/other/dfat/treaties/1976/22.html |date=2017-04-15 }}. Australasian Legal Information Institute, Australian Treaties Library. Retrieved on 15 April 2017.</ref> to launch a rocket from [[Woomera Test Range]]. The {{nowrap|Black Brant VB}} rocket was launched there on 9 November for experiments in the ionosphere.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Woomera |url=http://www.astronautix.com/w/woomera.html |access-date=2023-11-08 |website=Encyclopedia Astronautica|last=Wade|first=Mark}}</ref> Later, NASA would launch a number of {{nowrap|Black Brant IX}}.

At present, due to its 98% success rate, it remains one of the most popular sounding rockets ever built. The rockets have been used repeatedly by the [[Canadian Space Agency]] and NASA. There is a 1:1 scale model of the {{nowrap|Black Brant IX}} rocket in front of the head office of the Canadian Space Agency in Saint-Hubert, east of [[Montréal]]. A full-scale {{nowrap|Black Brant VC}} is on display in the Science Gallery of The [[Manitoba Museum]] in [[Winnipeg]], Manitoba, [[Canada]], and a Black Brant IV B replica is located at the [[Royal Aviation Museum of Western Canada]] also in Winnipeg.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-06-14 |title=Bristol Aerospace Black Brant IV B Sounding Rocket (Replica) - Royal Aviation Museum of Western Canada |url=https://www.royalaviationmuseum.com/aircraft/bristol-aerospace-black-brant-iv-b-sounding-rocket-replica/ |access-date=2026-07-10 |language=en-CA}}</ref>

In 1995, a Black Brant XII four-stage sounding rocket from the [[Andøya Rocket Range]] off the northwestern coast of Norway caused the [[Norwegian rocket incident]], also known as the Black Brant scare. The trajectory resembled that of a U.S. Navy submarine-launched [[Trident (missile)|Trident missile]]. Russian nuclear forces were put on high alert as a result, fearing a high-altitude nuclear attack that could blind Russian radar, and Russia's "nuclear briefcase", the [[Cheget]], was brought to Russian president [[Boris Yeltsin]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=Office |first=EUCOM History |title=This Week in EUCOM History: January 23-29, 1995 |url=http://www.eucom.mil/media-library/article/23042/this-week-in-eucom-history-january-23-29-1995 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160129002949/http://www.eucom.mil/media-library/article/23042/this-week-in-eucom-history-january-23-29-1995 |archive-date=2016-01-29 |access-date=2026-07-10 |website=www.eucom.mil |language=en-US}}</ref> who then had to decide whether to launch a retaliatory nuclear strike against the United States. It is the first and thus far only known incident where any nuclear-weapons state had its nuclear briefcase activated and prepared for launching an attack.

On September 19, 2009, a Black Brant XII that was launched to study clouds caused numerous calls from the northeastern U.S. reporting "strange lights in the sky". NASA reported that the light came from an artificial [[noctilucent cloud]] formed by the exhaust particles of the rocket's fourth stage at an altitude of about {{convert|278|km|mi|abbr=on}}.<ref>{{Cite web |title=CoptsUnited {{!}} NASA launches rocket, dozens report strange lights |url=http://www.coptsunited.com/Details.php?I=4&A=38 |access-date=2026-07-10 |website=www.coptsunited.com}}</ref>

The '''Cape Neddick Light''' is a [[lighthouse]] in [[Cape Neddick, Maine|Cape Neddick]], [[York, Maine|York]], [[Maine]].<ref name="cgll">{{cite book|title=Light List, Volume I, Atlantic Coast, St. Croix River, Maine to Shrewsbury River, New Jersey|author=United States Coast Guard|year=2009|page=2}}</ref><ref name="cghist">{{cite uscghist|ME|date=2009-08-08}}</ref> In 1874 [[United States Congress|Congress]] appropriated $15,000 to build a light station at the "Nubble" and in 1879 construction began. Cape Neddick Light Station was dedicated by the [[United States Lighthouse Service|U.S. Lighthouse Service]] and put into use in 1879. It is still in use today.

Plans had been in the works to build a lighthouse on the site since 1837. The tower is lined with brick and sheathed with [[cast iron]]. It stands {{convert|41|ft}} tall but the light is {{convert|88|ft}} above [[sea level]] because of the additional height of the steep rocky islet on which it sits. Unusually, the [[wiktionary:stanchions|stanchions]] of the walkway railing around the lantern room are decorated with {{convert|4|in|mm|adj=on}} brass replicas of the lighthouse itself.

==Location==
The Cape Neddick Light stands on Nubble Island about {{convert|100|yd}} off Cape Neddick Point. It is commonly known as "Nubble Light" or simply "the Nubble".

Cape Neddick Point is at the north end of Long Sands Beach in the village of York Beach. The lighthouse is inaccessible to the general public, but the nearby mainland is occupied by Sohier Park which offers many locations from which to view the lighthouse and a gift shop with a "Nubble" theme.

== Significance ==
Nubble Light is a famous [[United States|American]] icon and a classic example of a lighthouse. An image of the lighthouse is included on the [[Voyager Golden Record]] carried by the [[Voyager spacecraft]] as one of Earth's most prominent man-made structures or natural features, alongside features such as the [[Great Wall of China]] and the [[Taj Mahal]], to be viewed should it fall into the hands of intelligent extraterrestrials.<ref> {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131122011021/http://www.visitmaine.com/organization/301/ |date=2013-11-22 }}, ''visitmaine.org''</ref>

Cape Neddick Light is one of the last eight lights in Maine to still have its [[Fresnel lens]]. It was added to the [[National Register of Historic Places]] as '''Cape Neddick Light Station''' on April 16, 1985, reference number 85000844.

The lighthouse and island were featured in the movie ''[[Lost Boundaries]]'' (1949) starring [[Mel Ferrer]].

== Speculative history ==
Although the origin of the little lighthouse adornments is unknown, there are many other stories about the Nubble Light. Among them is the story of the keeper and his wife who, in 1912, decided to take advantage of the booming tourist business at the York beaches. They developed a lively business ferrying tourists across to the island and giving tours. The trade grew so lively that the light was neglected and the keeper fired.<ref></ref> Another keeper lived on the island with his {{convert|19|lb|adj=on}} cat who was an attraction in himself, especially when he reputedly swam across the channel to visit mainland friends. It is not always summer, though, and another story lends balance to lighthouse living. The Nubble is such a windy spot that in the winter, the temperature dropped so low that the flow of lamp oil to the incandescent oil vapor lamp was impeded. The problem was solved in 1938 when the lamp was electrified. That same year, the [[outhouse]] was closed, and the keeper and his family also received [[indoor plumbing]].

dp = p2 - p1
dl = math.radians(lon2 - lon1)
a = math.sin(dp/2)**2 + math.cos(p1)*math.cos(p2)*math.sin(dl/2)**2
D = 2*R*math.asin(math.sqrt(a))
print("Central angle: %.5f deg" % math.degrees(2*math.asin(math.sqrt(a))))

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Family of Canadian-designed sounding rockets

[![Image 4]]

Black Brant sounding rockets

The **Black Brant** is a family of [Canadian]-designed [sounding rockets] originally built by [Bristol Aerospace], since absorbed by [Magellan Aerospace] in [Winnipeg], Manitoba. Over 800 Black Brants of various versions have been launched since they were first produced in 1961, and the type remains one of the most popular sounding rockets.[[1]]#cite_note-1) They have been repeatedly used by the [Canadian Space Agency] and [NASA].

## History

[[edit]&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Black Brant was the result of research at [Canadian Armament Research and Development Establishment] (CARDE) during the 1950s into the nature of the upper part of the [atmosphere] as part of ongoing research into [anti-ballistic missile] systems and very-long-range communication. In 1957, CARDE contracted Bristol to produce a simple [rocket][fuselage], called the **Propulsion Test Vehicle**, for studies into high-power [solid fuels]. The resulting design, by [Albert Fia], was quite heavy, as it was designed to be able to accommodate a wide variety of engine burning times, propellant loadings and launch angles in keeping with its role as a test vehicle for ABM systems development. The first test flight took place only two years later from the [Churchill Rocket Research Range] in September 1959.[[2]]#cite_note-:0-2)

CARDE's attention later turned to long-distance communications and they found the _Propulsion Test Vehicle_ system useful as a [sounding rocket]. To better suit this role, Bristol modified the design to be lighter and more tailored to the sounding rocket role. This became the Black Brant,[[2]]#cite_note-:0-2) sharing the name with the [Black Brant] "Brant (goose)") goose. CARDE launched a number of Black Brant rockets over the next few years, both the original _Black Brant I_ design which could place a 68 kg (150 lb) payload to 150 km (93 mi) altitude, as well as the larger _Black Brant II_ which first flew in October 1960, and the smaller but higher-altitude _Black Brant III_.

The rocket's design emphasized reliability over payload and range.[[3]]#cite_note-ley196406-3) In July 1963 the much larger _Black Brant V_ first flew, which was also used as a booster stage for the _Black Brant III_ to make the _Black Brant IV_. The IV first flew in 1964, but failed, as did the next test launch. Aside from these two launches, which were corrected for, the Black Brant has never had another failure, making it one of the most reliable rockets in history. Since then it has undergone continual evolution, and the current versions are the XI and XII, consisting of Black Brant V used as an upper stage, with [Talos] and [Terrier] boosters as lower stages. They have reached altitudes of more than 1,500 km (930 mi), which is above the [ionosphere] and well above the orbits of the [Space Shuttle] and the [International Space Station].

The propellant designs developed by CARDE in the Black Brant program were the highest performing solid fuels of their day. Bristol then placed this propellant in a new 70 mm (2.8 in) rocket to form the [CRV7],[[4]]#cite_note-4) the first rocket capable of penetrating standard [Warsaw Pact] aircraft hangars. The CRV7 has since gone on to become the de facto standard rocket for most Western-aligned militaries.

In 1976, Australia and Canada through the [National Research Council Canada] (NRCC) agreed[[5]]#cite_note-5) to launch a rocket from [Woomera Test Range]. The Black Brant VB rocket was launched there on 9 November for experiments in the ionosphere.[[6]]#cite_note-6) Later, NASA would launch a number of Black Brant IX.

At present, due to its 98% success rate, it remains one of the most popular sounding rockets ever built. The rockets have been used repeatedly by the [Canadian Space Agency] and NASA. There is a 1:1 scale model of the Black Brant IX rocket in front of the head office of the Canadian Space Agency in Saint-Hubert, east of [Montréal]. A full-scale Black Brant VC is on display in the Science Gallery of The [Manitoba Museum] in [Winnipeg], Manitoba, [Canada], and a Black Brant IV B replica is located at the [Royal Aviation Museum of Western Canada] also in Winnipeg.[[7]]#cite_note-7)

In 1995, a Black Brant XII four-stage sounding rocket from the [Andøya Rocket Range] off the northwestern coast of Norway caused the [Norwegian rocket incident], also known as the Black Brant scare. The trajectory resembled that of a U.S. Navy submarine-launched [Trident missile] "Trident (missile)"). Russian nuclear forces were put on high alert as a result, fearing a high-altitude nuclear attack that could blind Russian radar, and Russia's "nuclear briefcase", the [Cheget], was brought to Russian president [Boris Yeltsin],[[8]]#cite_note-8) who then had to decide whether to launch a retaliatory nuclear strike against the United States. It is the first and thus far only known incident where any nuclear-weapons state had its nuclear briefcase activated and prepared for launching an attack.

On September 19, 2009, a Black Brant XII that was launched to study clouds caused numerous calls from the northeastern U.S. reporting "strange lights in the sky". NASA reported that the light came from an artificial [noctilucent cloud] formed by the exhaust particles of the rocket's fourth stage at an altitude of about 278 km (173 mi).[[9]]#cite_note-9)

**Wallops Flight Facility** (**WFF**; [IATA]: **WAL**, [ICAO]: **KWAL**, [FAA][LID]: **WAL**) is a [rocket launch site] on [Wallops Island] on the [Eastern Shore of Virginia], [United States], just east of the [Delmarva Peninsula] and approximately 100 miles (160 km) north-northeast of [Norfolk]. Since May 2026, the facility has been operated by the [John F. Kennedy Space Center] in [Merritt Island, Florida], having previously been operated by the [Goddard Space Flight Center] in [Greenbelt, Maryland][[1]]. WFF primarily serves to support science and exploration missions for [NASA] and other [federal agencies]. WFF includes an extensively instrumented range to support launches of more than a dozen types of [sounding rockets];[[2]] small expendable suborbital and orbital rockets;[[3]][high-altitude balloon] flights carrying scientific instruments for atmospheric and astronomical research; and, using its Research Airport, [flight tests] of aeronautical research aircraft, including [unmanned aerial vehicles].

There have been over 16,000 launches from the rocket testing range at Wallops since its founding in 1945 in the quest for information on the flight characteristics of airplanes, launch vehicles, and spacecraft, and to increase the knowledge of the Earth's upper atmosphere and the environment of [outer space]. The launch vehicles vary in size and power from the small [Super Loki] meteorological rockets to orbital-class vehicles.[[4]][[5]][[6]]

The Wallops Flight Facility also supports science missions for the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration] (NOAA) and occasionally for foreign governments and commercial organizations. Wallops also supports development tests and exercises involving [United States Navy] aircraft and ship-based electronics and weapon systems in the [Virginia Capes] operating area, near the entrance to the [Chesapeake Bay]. In addition to its fixed-location instrumentation assets, the WFF range includes mobile [radar], [telemetry] receivers, and command transmitters that can be transported by [cargo planes] to locations around the world, in order to establish a temporary range where no other instrumentation exists, to ensure safety, and to collect data in order to enable and support suborbital rocket launches from remote sites.

The WFF mobile range assets have been used to support rocket launches from locations in the Arctic and Antarctic regions, [South America], Africa, Europe, [Australia], and at sea. Workers at Wallops include approximately 1,000 full-time NASA [civil service] employees and the employees of contractors, about 30 [U.S. Navy] personnel, and about 100 employees of NOAA.

## History

[[edit]]

In 1945, NASA's predecessor agency, the [National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics] (NACA), established a rocket launch site on [Wallops Island] under the direction of the [Langley Research Center]. This site was designated the **Pilotless Aircraft Research Station** and conducted high-speed aerodynamic research to supplement wind tunnel and laboratory investigations into the problems of flight. In 1958, Congress established NASA, which absorbed Langley Research Center and other NACA field centers and research facilities. At that time, the Pilotless Aircraft Research Station became a separate facility, **Wallops Station**, operating directly under NASA Headquarters in Washington, D.C.

In 1959, NASA acquired the former **Naval Air Station Chincoteague**, and engineering and administrative activities were moved to this location. In 1974, the Wallops Station was named **Wallops Flight Center**. The name was changed to **Wallops Flight Facility** in 1981, when it became part of Goddard Space Flight Center.

In the early years, research at Wallops concentrated on obtaining aerodynamic data at transonic and low supersonic speeds. Between 1959 and 1961, Project Mercury[[7]] capsules were tested at Wallops in support of NASA's crewed space flight program – the [Mercury program] – before astronauts were launched from [Cape Canaveral Air Force Station] in Florida. Some of these tests using the [Little Joe] "Little Joe (rocket)")[booster rocket] were designed to [flight-qualify] components of the spacecraft, including the escape and recovery systems and some of the life support systems. Two rhesus monkeys, [Sam], launched in 1959, and Miss Sam, 1960, were sent aloft as pioneers for astronauts; both were recovered safely.

The first payload launched into orbit from Wallops Island was [Explorer IX], atop a [Scout rocket], on February 15, 1961.[[8]]

On September 6, 2013, the Lunar Atmosphere and Dust Environment Explorer ([LADEE]) was launched from Wallops, atop a [Minotaur V] rocket. This was the first time that an American lunar mission had been launched from anywhere but [Florida].[[9]]

In May 2026, [NASA Administrator][Jared Isaacman] announced that operational control of the Wallops Flight Facility would be moved from Goddard Space Flight Center to the John F. Kennedy Space Center.[[10]]

Wallops Island is currently experiencing [beach erosion] of 10 to 22 feet (3 to 7 meters) a year, due in part to the [current sea level rise]; some access roads and parking lots have had to be rebuilt several times over the past five years. NASA has responded by continually fortifying the shoreline with sand.[[11]]

A permanent ground control station for NASA's [RQ-4 Global Hawk] drone is at Wallops Flight Facility.[[12]]

## Facilities

[[edit]]

[![Image 8]]

The WFF Main Base is located on the Eastern Shore of Virginia on the [Delmarva Peninsula] about 5 miles (8.0 km) west of [Chincoteague, Virginia]; about 90 miles (140 km) north of [Norfolk, Virginia], and 40 miles (64 km) southeast of [Salisbury, Maryland]. The WFF consists of three separate parcels of land totaling 6,200 [acres] (25 km²): the Main Base, the Mainland, and the Wallops Island Launch Site. The Mainland and the Wallops Island Launch Site are about 7 miles (11 km) southeast of the Main Base.

### Airspace

[[edit]]

Wallops operates [controlled airspace] with [Federal Aviation Administration] (FAA) qualified [air traffic controllers] including:

* The WFF Airport Control Zone to 2,500 feet (760 m) within a 5-statute-mile (8.0 km) radius of the airport
* Restricted Area R-6604 connecting WFF airspace and offshore warning areas.

### Fixed facilities

[[edit]]

Major Wallops facilities include FAA-certified [runways]; an experimental UAV runway; and crash, fire, and rescue services. WFF has facilities for the receipt, inspection, assembly, checkout and storage of [rocket motors] and other hazardous [pyrotechnic devices]. The Wallops Island Launch Site includes six [launch pads], three [blockhouses] for launch control, and assembly buildings to support the preparation and launching of suborbital and orbital launch vehicles.

The '''Cape Neddick Light''' is a [[lighthouse]] in [[Cape Neddick, Maine|Cape Neddick]], [[York, Maine|York]], [[Maine]].<ref name="cgll">{{cite book|title=Light List, Volume I, Atlantic Coast, St. Croix River, Maine to Shrewsbury River, New Jersey|author=United States Coast Guard|year=2009|page=2}}</ref><ref name="cghist">{{cite uscghist|ME|date=2009-08-08}}</ref> In 1874 [[United States Congress|Congress]] appropriated $15,000 to build a light station at the "Nubble" and in 1879 construction began. Cape Neddick Light Station was dedicated by the [[United States Lighthouse Service|U.S. Lighthouse Service]] and put into use in 1879. It is still in use today.

Plans had been in the works to build a lighthouse on the site since 1837. The tower is lined with brick and sheathed with [[cast iron]]. It stands {{convert|41|ft}} tall but the light is {{convert|88|ft}} above [[sea level]] because of the additional height of the steep rocky islet on which it sits. Unusually, the [[wiktionary:stanchions|stanchions]] of the walkway railing around the lantern room are decorated with {{convert|4|in|mm|adj=on}} brass replicas of the lighthouse itself.

==Location==
The Cape Neddick Light stands on Nubble Island about {{convert|100|yd}} off Cape Neddick Point. It is commonly known as "Nubble Light" or simply "the Nubble".

Cape Neddick Point is at the north end of Long Sands Beach in the village of York Beach. The lighthouse is inaccessible to the general public, but the nearby mainland is occupied by Sohier Park which offers many locations from which to view the lighthouse and a gift shop with a "Nubble" theme.

== Significance ==
Nubble Light is a famous [[United States|American]] icon and a classic example of a lighthouse. An image of the lighthouse is included on the [[Voyager Golden Record]] carried by the [[Voyager spacecraft]] as one of Earth's most prominent man-made structures or natural features, alongside features such as the [[Great Wall of China]] and the [[Taj Mahal]], to be viewed should it fall into the hands of intelligent extraterrestrials.<ref> {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131122011021/http://www.visitmaine.com/organization/301/ |date=2013-11-22 }}, ''visitmaine.org''</ref>

Cape Neddick Light is one of the last eight lights in Maine to still have its [[Fresnel lens]]. It was added to the [[National Register of Historic Places]] as '''Cape Neddick Light Station''' on April 16, 1985, reference number 85000844.

The lighthouse and island were featured in the movie ''[[Lost Boundaries]]'' (1949) starring [[Mel Ferrer]].

== Speculative history ==
Although the origin of the little lighthouse adornments is unknown, there are many other stories about the Nubble Light. Among them is the story of the keeper and his wife who, in 1912, decided to take advantage of the booming tourist business at the York beaches. They developed a lively business ferrying tourists across to the island and giving tours. The trade grew so lively that the light was neglected and the keeper fired.<ref></ref> Another keeper lived on the island with his {{convert|19|lb|adj=on}} cat who was an attraction in himself, especially when he reputedly swam across the channel to visit mainland friends. It is not always summer, though, and another story lends balance to lighthouse living. The Nubble is such a windy spot that in the winter, the temperature dropped so low that the flow of lamp oil to the incandescent oil vapor lamp was impeded. The problem was solved in 1938 when the lamp was electrified. That same year, the [[outhouse]] was closed, and the keeper and his family also received [[indoor plumbing]].
